But Mr. Hannis, of course, I would remind you of the well settled [realtime transcript read in error "subtle"] procedure that you let the witness read it himself and then you formulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I guess I should have allowed you to read that to yourself and ask you if that refreshes your recollection about what you've said, but since I've now read it out loud, could you tell us if that refreshes your recollection about what you told them at the time?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked with you and when we talked about it, about this, I indicated the corrections which I had after the first interview. And in the correction I objected because I said that I had informed them about paramilitaries, provided information about what they did -- about what I heard about what they did. I think you have those corrections too, so about what I had heard not about what I had seen. As for the rest, it can stand as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement at the time you said you could hear all this from time to time, that the paramilitaries came until -- and that people had been locked up and that people had been killed. That's what you heard; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 42 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we go on, if I may, there's an intervention on the record. I see at line 7, page 67, I am quoted as referring to subtle procedure, whereas it should be well settled, s-e-t-t-l-e-d, procedure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at page 42, line 5, after asking you about what you reported at the meeting, Mr. Cvijetic asked you: "After that you noticed Mr. Zugic from MUP was there, although you didn't know what capacity he was in and he was in the territory of Zvornik municipality and he was actually compiling this type of information." Could you look at paragraph 131 in your statement and read what it says there and tell us if that refreshes your recollection about when you noticed Mr. Zugic in Zvornik for the first time.

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement I said that he arrived in late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to disagree with that now?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean? In what sense? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anything you've seen or read or heard since then that makes you think it's some different date other than late May?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I'm not sure absolutely about the dates. I cannot be sure now that those are the dates, but I'm sure that he came after that meeting. I don't know what is important there, whether for me to remember what day it was. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, I have a couple of short questions to you. And one of the questions that I have relate to the testimony that you gave us about the curfew in Zvornik at the time. A document was introduced to you by Mr. Cvijetic, and I think it was assigned Exhibit 1D377, and I would ask the Registrar to bring it up on the screen. Thank you. Do you recall the document, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the document, but I said that the decision existed. I don't remember this document in this form, but I do recall that a decision was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. My question goes to the implementation of this decision, and I would like you to explain to us --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the witness, he isn't able to see the decision that you're talking about on his monitor. Perhaps it can be put up again on the screen so he can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Cvijetic, and thank you because also in the English version it's the wrong document that came up. Yes, this is the right document dealing with the curfew. Mr. Witness, what I'm interested in is if you could tell us how this curfew was implemented in practice, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the Crisis Staff until the 10th of April for two days longer was I a member of the Crisis Staff. So this wasn't even begun to be implemented. The implementation of the decision began only after the Serbian forces entered Zvornik, and I think that it was implemented by the mixed composition, meaning the Territorial Defence and policemen. I think there were also soldiers participating. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you recall from your own experience at the time how the curfew was implemented in practice? I mean, were people really prevented from getting out of their houses from 9.00 in the evening until 5.00 the next morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: (redacted). But I have to say generally the people avoided going out at night of their own accord, not that someone was preventing them from doing so. At any point during the day there were armed people in the streets monitoring the citizens. For example, at one time during the day two people in military uniforms came up to me and they asked to see my documents. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And for what purpose would they do that?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to check my identity. At least that's how I understood it. Do you have ID? Where do you live? That kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what were they looking for? Who were they looking for in particular? Why would they be interested in your identity?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they were ordered to do that, to patrol the streets and to check the IDs of people, to check who was out in the streets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if any permissions to exit your house after 9.00 and between 5.00 in the morning were issued to particular groups of people?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I'm not sure about that. I couldn't confirm that, no. I'm not ruling out that this did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And was the curfew to your knowledge applied equally to Serbs as well as to non-Serbs in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These things applied to everything, to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we can see on the screen, that it applies without distinction to all citizens. But my question to you is rather if you know whether it was also applied in practice equally to everyone.

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was very dangerous for people in that period, that April, for people who were recognised or identified as Muslims, they could have been checked in the sense of their IDs could have been checked or they could have been taken to some other place for a greater degree of control. But there is another problem here, if I may be permitted to continue. In that time the problem was that other than the organs which you could say had some degree of legal basis, the TO and similar, there were also persons from unknown units, from unknown forces who started setting up check-points, paramilitary check-points, who were doing checks of the population of their own accord. That was the big problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now that you raise it, your testimony begs the question of whether the paramilitary units that were manning these check-points were also required to withdraw at 9.00 p.m. every day and not show up until 5.00 the next morning. Do you recall how that was? Were the check-points empty and not manned during the night-times?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning the check-points in town were functioning I think. I personally, for example, went out at night rarely, so I really couldn't tell you where they were, how many. But I think that there were check-points in town. I think that at the beginning of May all the check-points were removed, the Territorial Defence dismantled them all but couldn't dismantle the ones that were at exit points of the municipality that were on the outer edges of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Could I just get back to your testimony to me just a short while ago, where you said that people who had been recognised or identified as Muslims could be taken to some other place for a greater degree of control. Did you mean to say that this was a practice that was applied only to non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard of several cases where people were literally taken from the street, but this was never done by members of the police or the regular forces of the Territorial Defence; this was done by the paramilitaries. For many people it was never known what their fate was. Some were picked up on the street, some at the check-points. In the Zvornik municipality this was a period of considerable lawlessness and a period when the paramilitary forces were stronger than anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This brings me to the second question that I wanted to put to you. You testified earlier this afternoon that in response to questions put to you by Counsel Cvijetic that Zvornik was, so to say, had become a state in the state. And I think this was indeed the point that counsel wanted to establish. And I would wish you to elaborate a little more on this point because what I understood from your testimony is that there was, as you have just said, a considerable degree of lawlessness in the early days after the 8th of April, 1992, in Zvornik and that the arrival of paramilitary units that acted more or less on their own authority tended to create this situation of lawlessness. So it was very much a de facto situation in which it was difficult to keep control of what was happening in Zvornik and surrounding areas. But to say that there was lawlessness in the streets of Zvornik and then from that fact to conclude that Zvornik had become a state in the state seems to me to be two versions that are quite far apart, because even if there were lawlessness in the streets there still might have been a state and the Republika Srpska had already been established. And maybe it had difficulties in controlling the activities in all the areas within its territory, but it certainly hadn't disappeared. And I guess that even though there was lawlessness in the streets of Zvornik, the authorities of Zvornik would still recognise the authority of the Republika Srpska, would they not? So my question to you is really: Can you describe in some more detail exactly what you mean when you said that Zvornik had become a state in the state? And what I'm particularly interested in is not only the factual situation but also the legal situation, if you can provide us with an appreciation of this.

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire series of documents that we could see today and yesterday indicate that the municipality was practically cut off from the centre, that it didn't have communication with the centre, that it didn't have anything to rely on in terms of internal organisation. And that practically there was a lot of chaos and lawlessness, there was war all around, a lot of shooting, everyone was armed, the majority was armed, and there were many groups acting on their own. And it was very difficult to control them. The Crisis Staff which transformed into the temporary government was attempting to strengthen the Territorial Defence which the temporary government tried later by appointing a commander and issuing other orders practically from the inside without contact with the military or Republika Srpska. Regulations were adopted ranging from how to pay out retirement benefits, how to establish courts, how to finance people who were in the Territorial Defence, and even under pressure the paramilitaries were paid as well because the temporary government had to do that as well, care for the refugees. So there was a vacuum, empty space where the state was unable to intervene. Why? Because the state itself was out there. Republika Srpska didn't have a history of 20 or 30 years back; it was created in three or four months. It was all blank. This person from the Ministry of Internal Affairs wasn't able to send somebody to help or the one from the army because they didn't have those things.

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). So somebody would be working there incognito without being appointed for that particular post. So I don't know if you understand me, if I'm being quite clear, and that is why I said this about Zvornik. But it wasn't only Zvornik. There were many municipalities that were like a state within a state because the municipalities were left to themselves. Up until the moment that the central government managed to organise itself, to organise the army, to set up the ministries, and then to embark on action; before that, this wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see and you have explained it very well. I just wanted to ensure that when you said that Zvornik was a state within the state, that this did not mean that there was any attempt from Zvornik to denounce the authority of the Republika Srpska and to become independent and not -- no longer wishing to obey the orders or the instructions that came out of the Republika Srpska. That was not the case. It was a practical deficiency, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only practical deficiency. I've just explained to you that the RS itself had been created only a few months earlier. So there was no continuity. We're not talking about a state that had been there for a while, that had laws, institutions, that were all functioning well, and so on. We were all in a vacuum and nobody knew what to do in practice. April was a month of utter lawlessness and chaos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And for approximately how long did this situation last? You mentioned several dates, end of May, July, August. How -- I know it's difficult because it was probably a phase in which the lawlessness gradually was phased out, but can you clarify a bit if you can.

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said here even today I think that from the moment of the arrival of the special unit and the rest of these people, the situation in Zvornik changed dramatically. The situation was completely different from what it had been before until that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the brigade arrived on 30th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documents that we've seen, the brigade was supposed to be established on the 30th of May. But the problem with its establishment and its manning were -- was around for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question based on Judge Harhoff's questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Further Re-examination by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, after the arrest of the Yellow Wasps and the other paramilitaries in late July when you say things got better, the police got organised, the military got organised, the governmental authorities were able to be more organised, are you aware of any cases in Zvornik where members of those units were prosecuted in Zvornik or the Republika Srpska for crimes they committed against non-Serbs? Any of Pivarski's men, Zuco's men, Simo Chetnik's men, Crni's men, Captain Dragan's men, any of those guys get prosecuted in the Republika Srpska for crimes allegedly committed against non-Serbs that you know of?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you briefly. They were investigated against on -- the police went out to search for them after the arrival of the special unit, and I know that they were in prison in Bijeljina. I know that they were interrogated by one of the judges, but they were released. I'm not sure after how much time. And the story was for a while that they were released because somebody from Yugoslavia had intervened. When I spoke to the Defence counsel, he showed me some documents that convinced me that these people had been treated judicially. Maybe not until the end as it should have been, but they were treated or processed judicially. And he had documents to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which people and where? Are you talking about Zuco and his brother in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yellow Wasps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anybody else and anybody in the Republika Srpska, prosecuted in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ST-215 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't have any concrete information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness, for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, the Chamber wishes to render its oral decision on a couple of matters that have been brought before us. The first issue is the confidential Prosecution motion which was filed on 11th of August, 2010, and the corrigendum filed on 20th of August, requesting to amend the Rule 92 ter package for Witness ST-004 by adding a one-page supplemental statement obtained from the witness on the 23rd of June, 2010, and to have also added two associated documents, namely, Rule 65 ter number 2116, which is a list of reserve police officers for a specific police station, and 65 ter number 2117, which is a list of employees of the SJB for that area. And on the 24th of August, 2010, the Defence jointly responded objecting to the Prosecution's motion. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the supplemental statement is prima facie relevant and has probative value. It was disclosed to the Defence at the latest in early August. And as ST-004 is not yet scheduled to give testimony, the Trial Chamber considers that sufficient notice has been given to the Defence. Any prejudice to the Defence by the admission of the one-page supplemental statement to this witness's 92 ter package is therefore negligible. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber notes that the two associated documents form an inseparable and indispensable part of the supplemental statement which they accompany. So for the foregoing reasons and in the interests of justice, the Trial Chamber hereby allows the amendment of ST-004's Rule 92 ter package as requested by the Prosecution and the adding of the supplemental statement to the Prosecution's 65 ter list of exhibits. The Trial Chamber will consider admission into evidence of the entire package of Witness ST-004 under Rule 92 ter at the conclusion of his testimony. So that was one decision. And the other decision which the Chamber wishes to render is in respect of the so-called law library, and the decision reads as follows. The Chamber is seized of the Defence and Prosecution joint motion for admission of agreed documents constituting what we would now wish to term as the reference library filed on 25th of August, 2010, in which the parties agreed on the admission into evidence of decisions, laws, and regulations of the SFRY and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Republika Srpska. Pursuant to Rule 89(C) and (D) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that these documents which are listed in Annex A of the motion are relevant and have probative value and hereby admits them into evidence. However, the Chamber orders the Registrar to ensure that the items in the reference library are properly registered and assigned exhibit numbers as a separate category so as to ensure that they are kept separate from Prosecution exhibits, Defence exhibits, and Chamber's exhibits. We propose that they be classified as exhibits under, for instance, the letter R for reference library, but we leave that to the Registrar. Thank you very much. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And with -- sorry, Mr. Hannis, you were about to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I was just rising in anticipation of your rising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If memory serves, the last time I looked at the court schedule we are in this courtroom for the remainder of the week, alternating mornings to afternoons. So we would reconvene at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.
